Title: The Royal Statutes of the Barrowmark

[The beginning of this book is pages upon pages describing the holdings belonging to the march, followed by a lengthy talk about the saints and justice.]

Title First, of Servitude

All may lawfully hold others in service, under conditions prescribed by the fair lord, so long as justice and order are maintained.

1. Servitude is lawful when entered into by conquest, debt, or judgment of the lord.
2. Those in servitude shall owe obedience to their master and perform the duties assigned, while masters owe protection and sustenance sufficient for life.
3. Servants may not bear arms, hold office, or claim legal standing independent of their master.
4. Release from servitude, may occur by the will of the master, payment of debt, or at the lord’s decree.
5. The laws of inheritance and commerce shall respect the station of those in servitude, and masters may pass servitude to heirs or transfer by lawful contract.

Title Second, of Duels

Let it be known that disputes of honor or grave matters may be tried by duel.

1. The noble may refuse challenges of the lowborn.
2. Duels shall be fought before witnesses on ground appointed by the lord.
3. Either party may fight by champion.
4. No hidden sorcery, poison, nor device shall be brought into combat.
5. Once a combatant yields or becomes unable to continue fighting, the victor shall be held as proven and his word true under the eyes of the saints.
6. To slay one who surrenders is murder, unless the duel was sworn to the death.
7. To refuse a duel is to insult the standing of the challenger; the refuser may not seek protection of the law, should the challenger take fair action to defend their honor.

Title Third, of Infamy

All subjects shall speak the truth, keep faith, and abide by the law, lest they be branded infamous.

1. Infamy is the state of one who has broken faith or law, and thereby is cast outside the trust and protection of the fair lord.
2. The infamous shall have no standing in the lord's courts: they may not bring suit, bear oath, serve as lawful witness, nor claim the lord's safe-conduct, warrant, or aid in pleas.
3. Those of standing are not forbidden from dealing with the infamous; merchants and private persons may trade with them at their own peril. Yet the lord’s officers shall not enforce contracts, recover debts, nor uphold warranties made for the benefit of one of infamous station
4. The declaration of infamy shall be made openly by the fair lord or his sworn officers, that all may know and bear witness to the loss of standing.
5. Knowingly sheltering, aiding, or abetting an infamous individual, may cast suspicion on those of good standing.
6. Repentance and restitution may restore standing, according to the judgment of the lord.

Title Fourth, of Killing

There shall be three kinds of killing: by accident, in self-defense, and in murder without cause.

1. Those who take a life by accident shall be free of guilt, provided they have taken all precautions to prevent such fate.
2. Self-defense is no crime if not the first blow, whether in one’s house, in battle, or against assailants.
3. Murder done without cause, in malice or envy, shall be punished as the lord or their sworn officer decrees.
4. Those who kill by command of the Lord are blameless.
5. Whosoever strikes, maims, or batters another without cause or lawful right shall be guilty of assault.

Title Fifth, of Theft

None shall take what is not theirs.

1. Whoever takes coin, goods, or chattels without leave is a thief.
2. Those who aid or harbor a thief shall be judged accomplices.
3. Theft committed by force, stealth, or deception shall be judged accordingly.
4. That which is seized by the lord or agents thereof shall not be considered theft.

Title Sixth, of Sorcery and Heresy

Magic is a power most perilous, and shall be wielded only in service of God and the saints.

1. No perilous or unlawful sorcery shall be wrought within any town, village, or hold of the march.
2. Unlawful sorcery is any magic that goes against the saints.
3. None shall blaspheme against God or the saints, deny their miracles, or scorn the holy sacraments, lest they be judged heretic.
4. It is the right of the church to involve itself in judgement of heretics.

Title Seventh, of Punishment

These are the punishments the fair lord suggests to be used for those who transgress the laws of the realm, according to the severity of their offense.

1. For minor offenses: A warning, restitution of goods or coin, or service to the lord may suffice.
2. For offenses: Fines, public shaming, such as pillorying or being paraded across town, or corporal punishment, such as flogging, may be imposed.
3. For great or violent offenses: Imprisonment, severe corporal punishment, such as amputation of limbs, exile, or death may be applied.
4. Heresy: The church shall judge the heretic, and the lord may impose additional punishment should circumstances require it.
